title-group.article-title: The Association between Intranasal Esketamine and Treatment- emergent Insomnia in the Treatment of Treatment-resistant Major Depression: A Meta-analysis

sec.title: Objective
sec.p: Intranasal (IN) esketamine represents a novel add-on treatment for treatment-resistant depression (TRD) with reported favourable effects on insomnia. IN esketamine treatment might similarly reduce the incidence of insomnia as an adverse event (AE). The present meta-analysis therefore investigated whether IN esketamine relative to placebo is associated with a lower incidence of insomnia as an AE in adults with TRD.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Data were retrieved from seven randomised placebo-controlled trials evaluating the safety and efficacy of IN esketamine combined with a monoaminergic antidepressant in the treatment of TRD that reported data on insomnia as an AE. The study population (n = 1,311) comprised adult patients (aged ≥ 18 years) with a primary diagnosis of major depressive disorder. A mixed-effects logistic regression model was employed to compare the incidence of insomnia as an AE between the IN esketamine and placebo group.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Insomnia as an AE was reported by 52 patients (7.3%) in the IN esketamine group relative to 40 (6.7%) in the placebo group. IN esketamine compared to placebo was not associated with the odds of insomnia as an AE (OR = 1.07; 95% CI = 0.68−1.69; p = 0.76). There was no evidence for heterogeneity between the included trials.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: IN esketamine does not affect the occurrence of insomnia as an AE in the treatment of TRD. This contrasts previous findings demonstrating beneficial effects of esketamine on insomnia severity relative to placebo, although AE reporting may not capture insomnia improvements in a population with frequent baseline insomnia.

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a highly prevalent psychiatric disorder that affects 280 million people worldwide, representing the second leading cause of disease burden [1]. While many patients with MDD can be effectively treated with traditional psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy, about one-third do not achieve remission, even after multiple steps of antidepressant treatment [2]. These patients are considered to have treatment-resistant depression (TRD), commonly defined as the absence of a clinically meaningful response following the consecutive treatment with two antidepressant agents, provided at adequate dose and treatment duration [3].

The non-competitive N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor antagonist ketamine has recently been introduced as an efficacious, rapid-acting treatment for patients with TRD. An intranasal (IN) formulation of esketamine, the (S)-enantiomer of racemic ketamine, has been approved for clinical application in TRD. Meta-analyses demonstrate that 30 to 70% of patients respond, and 20 to 50% of the patients remit following IN esketamine treatment [4-6]. While efficacious in a proportion of the patients, the mechanisms contributing to variable treatment outcomes remain largely unclear.

Increasing evidence suggests that a reduction in insomnia severity following esketamine treatment may contribute to its antidepressant efficacy. Insomnia is characterized by difficulties initiating and maintaining sleep, coinciding with daytime dysfunction. Insomnia comprises the most common sleep disturbance in MDD, contributing to the aetiology [7] and an unfavourable clinical course [8], although results are variable [9-12]. In relation, behavioural and pharmacological treatments that directly target insomnia have been found to improve treatment outcomes in MDD [13]. Recent studies demonstrated that (es)ketamine treatment improves subjective and objective measures of sleep quality, including insomnia [14-17]. Moreover, both insomnia severity at baseline and improvements in insomnia severity during treatment have been associated with antidepressant efficacy in the treatment in TRD with (es)ketamine [15,18].

Clinical trials in MDD and TRD frequently include an assessment of insomnia as an adverse event (AE). Meta-analyses have observed that most second-generation antidepressants, with the exception of agomelatine, are associated with increased odds of insomnia as an AE compared to placebo [19,20], occurring in approximately 5 to 10% of patients [21]. Considering the reported favourable effects of (es)ketamine on insomnia, IN esketamine treatment might reduce the incidence of insomnia as an AE. A recent meta-analysis by Wang et al. [22] investigated AEs following IN esketamine treatment but did not assess insomnia as an AE. The present meta-analysis aimed to complement this meta-analysis by investigating the association between IN esketamine treatment and the incidence of insomnia as an AE.

sec.title: Data
sec.p: Data were retrieved from studies included in a recent meta-analysis evaluating the safety and efficacy of IN esketamine [22]. Seven randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials reporting data on insomnia as an AE were included [23-29]. The included clinical trials used a non-systematic assessment of insomnia as an AE. All studies defined an AE as “any untoward medical occurrence in a participant who received study drug without regard to possibility of causal relationship,” except for two trials [23,24], which did not disclose a definition for an AE.

sec.title: Study Population
sec.p: The study population (n = 1,311) comprised adult patients (aged ≥18 years) with a primary diagnosis of MDD according to the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders fourth or fifth edition [30]. Patients diagnosed with MDD with psychotic features, bipolar (or related) disorder(s), obsessive compulsive disorder, antisocial personality disorder, borderline personality disorder, intellectual disability, or psychotic disorder were excluded from participation in all of the included trials.

sec.title: Data Extraction
sec.p: The primary outcome comprised the frequency of reported insomnia as an AE in the IN esketamine and placebo groups. C.T. and A.Z. independently extracted the data using a predefined extraction sheet. The resulting dataset comprised the number of participants with and without insomnia as an AE in each treatment arm across the included randomized controlled trials (RCTs).

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: The association between IN esketamine and insomnia was investigated using the same mixed-effects logistic regression model as in a recent meta-analysis assessing antidepressant treatment-emergent insomnia in children and adolescents with MDD [31]. Random intercepts and slopes for the treatment dummy variable were included at the study level to account for differences in the overall prevalence of insomnia and differences in the treatment effect across studies. Based on the model, the estimated pooled prevalence of insomnia for participants receiving antidepressants relative to placebo, the pooled odds ratio (OR), and corresponding 95% Wald-type confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. Evidence for heterogeneity in the treatment effect was assessed through a likelihood ratio test, comparing the model with and without the random treatment effect. Due to the small number of trials (k < 10), an evaluation of publication bias was not deemed meaningful [32]. All statistical analyses were conducted using R version 4.4.2 (R Core Team) with the lme4 [33] and metafor [34] packages.

sec.title: Study Characteristics
sec.p: Table 1 presents the study characteristics of the included RCTs. In total, 1,311 subjects (mean age = 45.86 years; 63% women) were included in the meta-analysis. The double-blind phase lasted four weeks in all trials except for one, which lasted two weeks [24]. In all of the included RCTs, IN esketamine (dose range 14−84 mg) was administered in addition to traditional, monoaminergic antidepressant treatment.

sec.title: Effect of Intranasal Esketamine on Insomnia as an Adverse Event
sec.p: Insomnia as an AE was reported by 52 patients (7.3%) in the IN esketamine group relative to 40 (6.7%) in the placebo group. Results demonstrated that IN esketamine compared to placebo was not associated with the odds of insomnia as an AE (OR = 1.07; 95% CI = 0.68−1.69; p = 0.76). There was no evidence for heterogeneity between the RCTs (χ2 = 0.09, df = 2, p = 0.96). Figure 1 presents a forest plot summarizing the effects of esketamine treatment on insomnia reported as an AE.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: The present meta-analysis investigated the association between IN esketamine and insomnia as an AE in the treatment of TRD. The results demonstrated no significant difference in the incidence of insomnia as an AE between the IN esketamine and placebo group, indicating that IN esketamine is neither associated with a higher nor lower risk of treatment-emergent insomnia. The observation that 7.3% of patients reported treatment-emergent insomnia during IN esketamine treatment corresponds with findings from a meta-analysis of traditional antidepressants, which estimated that treatment-emergent insomnia occurs in 5 to 10% of patients [21]. The absence of an association between IN esketamine treatment and treatment-emergent insomnia, however, contrasts prior evidence demonstrating that (es)ketamine treatment reduces insomnia severity [14-16,35].

Several potential explanations could account for this divergent finding. First, spontaneous AE reporting may lack sensitivity to capture reductions in insomnia, as it is prone to new or worsening symptoms rather than improvements. Of note, around 65% of the TRD patients included in clinical trials on IN esketamine reported moderate-to-severe insomnia at baseline [16], limiting the detection of insomnia improvements assessed as an AE. Nonetheless, previous meta-analyses support the value of insomnia as an AE to detect both favourable and unfavourable effects of monoaminergic antidepressants on insomnia [19,20]. Second, many types of medication commonly used in the treatment of MDD and TRD, including (second-generation) antidepressants and benzodiazepines, can positively or negatively affect insomnia. As the clinical trials included in this meta-analysis permitted the continuation of other psychotropic compounds (Table 1), it is possible that any effect of IN esketamine on insomnia was confounded by the effects of concomitant medication.

sec.title: Limitations and Future Directions
sec.p: The present meta-analysis has several limitations. First, the assessment of insomnia as an AE may lack sensitivity to detect improvements in insomnia. Hence, standardized and systematic approaches such as psychometric questionnaires, polysomnography, or actigraphy may provide greater ability in detecting favourable effects on insomnia. Second, IN esketamine dosages in the included RCTs ranged from 14 to 84 mg/day, which could have influenced the incidence of insomnia as an AE. Dose-dependent effects of (es)ketamine on sleep architecture have been described in preclinical studies [36,37] and future studies are needed to determine whether a similar relationship exists for insomnia. Of note, due to the limited number of trials, an analysis of dose-dependent effects on insomnia was not feasible. Third, clinical trials published between the initial meta-analysis [22] and the present study were not included in the present meta-analysis, since this meta-analysis is specifically intended to complement the previous meta-analysis on AEs [22]. Fourth, one of the original eight studies did not report insomnia as an AE and was therefore excluded from the present analysis, reducing the sample size and statistical power. Finally, in all of the included trials, IN esketamine was combined with other psychotropic medication, including monoaminergic antidepressants, antipsychotics, and mood stabilizers, that might have influenced insomnia incidence. Given the limited number of studies and restricted variation in concomitant medication, subgroup analysis was not meaningful and warrants further research in patient-level meta-analyses.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In conclusion, IN esketamine does not affect the incidence of insomnia as an AE during the acute treatment of TRD. IN esketamine therefore neither appears to have a protective nor a harmful effect on treatment-emergent insomnia, although AE reporting may not capture insomnia improvements in a population characterized by high baseline insomnia.
